title: Forming Capital Letters
keyIdea: Capital letters are tall: every capital touches the top line and sits on the base line, and none hang below it. Start each line at the top and pull down, go across from left to right, and start slanted lines at the top too. C and O start near the top and go over to the left. A well-made capital is tall, sits on the line and faces the right way.

kid: Capital letters are the big letters. Each one is tall. It goes from the top line down to the base line. Small letters are not all tall. Small e stops at the dashed line. Small g and p hang down below the line. Capitals never hang down.
Most capitals are made of lines. Put your pencil on the top line and pull down. Then lift it. Lines across go from left to right, the way you read. L is a line down, then a line across.
Slanted lines start at the top too. A has two slants that slide down from a point at the top. Then a line goes across the middle.

C and O are round. Start near the top. Go over the top to the left and round. D is a line down, then a curve round to the right. Check each capital. Is it tall? Does it sit on the line? Does it face the right way?
adult: This topic, for ages 5 to 6, is about forming all 26 capital letters correctly so that writing is legible. Children learn three things: capitals are all the same height, from the top line to the base line, with no descenders; each stroke starts in the right place and goes in the right direction; and capitals look different from their lowercase partners.

The usual rules in UK and US handwriting schemes are: start at the top, pull downward strokes towards you, draw horizontal strokes left to right, start slanted strokes at the top, and draw C, G, O and Q anticlockwise from near the top. D, B, P and R add their curves after the straight down stroke, going round to the right. Schemes differ in the order of some strokes, such as the bar of T, so the lab checks where each stroke starts and which way it goes rather than one fixed order.

Common mistakes: starting down strokes at the bottom, drawing O and C clockwise, writing capitals the same height as small letters, letting capitals hang below the line like g and p, and reversing letters such as N, S, J and Z. Reversals are normal at this age and fade with practice. Be careful to praise clear letters, not perfect ones.

In the lab your child finds the capital in five pairs on the writing lines, traces L and E from green start dots, then the slants in A and X, then the curves in C, O and D, and finally picks the well-made capital from look-alikes that are too short, floating, sinking or back to front.

familyTip: Write your child's name with a capital first letter on lined paper and let them trace over it. Ask "Where do we start?" before each letter. Use big movements first: draw capitals in the air, in sand or with a finger on a steamy window, starting at the top every time.

practice.prompt: Which one is a capital letter?
practice.hint: A capital is tall and touches the top line.
practice.explain: B is the capital. Small b and small d have a short tummy low down.

practice.prompt: You write {n} capital L letters in a row. Where does each long line start?
practice.hint: Put your pencil on the top line first.
practice.explain: All {n} long lines start at the top line and pull down. Then the short line goes across.

practice.prompt: Which way does the line go across the bottom of L?
practice.hint: Lines across go the same way you read.
practice.explain: The line across goes left to right, the same way we read.

practice.prompt: Mia writes {n} capital O letters. Which way should each one go round?
choices: Start near the top, go over to the left
Start at the bottom, go to the right
practice.hint: O goes round the same way as C.
practice.explain: Each of the {n} O letters starts near the top and goes over the top to the left, then all the way round.

practice.prompt: Small p hangs below the line. What about capital P?
practice.explain: Capital P sits on the base line and touches the top line. Only small p hangs down.

pool.prompt: How tall is every capital letter?
choices: From the top line to the base line
pool.explain: Every capital goes from the top line to the base line. The dashed line is for small letters like e.

pool.prompt: Where do the two slanted lines of A start?
choices: At the point at the top
pool.hint: Slanted lines start at the top too.
pool.explain: Both slants of A start at the point at the top and slide down. Then the middle line goes across.

choices: Over the top to the left
pool.explain: C starts near the top and goes over to the left and round, the same as O.

pool.prompt: Sam writes his name {n} times. Which letter should be the capital?
pool.hint: A name starts with a capital.
pool.explain: Each of the {n} times, Sam starts with a capital S. The a and m are small.

pool.prompt: Ben's N looks like a mirror picture. What is wrong?
pool.hint: Check which way the slant goes.
pool.explain: A back to front N faces the wrong way. In N the slant goes from the top left down to the bottom right.

pool.prompt: Kim makes D. She draws the line down first. Which way does the curve go?
choices: From the top, round to the right
From the top, round to the left
From the bottom, up and round
pool.hint: The curve of D bulges out on the right.
pool.explain: D's curve starts at the top of the line and goes round to the right, down to the base line.

pool.prompt: You draw {n} lines across for capital E letters. Which way does each one go?
pool.hint: Lines across go the way you read.
pool.explain: All {n} lines across go left to right, the way we read.

pool.prompt: Which capital letter is made only of straight lines?
pool.hint: Look for a letter with no curves.
pool.explain: E is a line down and three lines across. O and S are curvy.

visual.caption: Only straight lines, or a curve too? Drag each capital, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: spot capitals, trace straight, slanted and curvy capitals from the start dot, and pick the well-made one.
